idiom_name: nested step interfaces + one private Steps class + static builder() entry point
implementation_notes: This is the canonical realization: nested step interfaces declare only the next step's method, one private implementation class implements them all, a private constructor plus a static entry point fix the first step, and build() is declared only on the final interface so an incomplete chain has no build method to call. Validation belongs in build() - the pattern enforces presence and order, never value correctness - and effective-interface design keeps the intermediate methods invisible because callers only ever see the interface returned by the previous step. Use it where the order is a real invariant (request/DSL builders, credential setup); where only optional parameters proliferate, the plain builder of Effective Java Item 2 with a single builder() entry is the simpler relative.
pitfalls: If the factory returns the implementation class (or the class is public), callers can declare it and start the chain at any step; return the first step interface and keep the implementation private.

Modelling repeatable optional steps is the subtle part: once a step method returns the final interface, the optional methods must be on that final interface (or on an interface it extends), otherwise a second optional call is unavailable.

Java records expose a public canonical constructor: building a record through a staged builder still requires making that constructor private (or using the class form), otherwise the staging is bypassed.
Duplicating required-field checks in every setter instead of validating in build() hides cross-field rules and makes the stage types look stronger than they are.
